paper.title: External validation of an artificial intelligence-based ECG algorithm for the early diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction: a prospective diagnostic cohort study.
paper.abstract:
Background: A novel artificial intelligence-based electrocardiogram (AI-ECG) model (AiTiA MI v2.00.00) for the early diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction (AMI) was developed using data from Korean patients. Its performance in a European population remains unknown.
Methods: Patients presenting to the emergency department (ED) with suspected AMI were enrolled in two prospective European cohorts (APACE & APACE-Light; ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT00470587). The primary outcome was AMI, centrally adjudicated according to the fourth Universal Definition of MI. The AI-ECG model was applied to 12-lead ECGs recorded at ED presentation. Its diagnostic performance for AMI was directly compared to that of the BASEL score, high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T (hs-cTnT), the recalibrated HEART score (all at ED presentation), and integrated physician judgment at 90 min, with the last two only available in APACE. Predefined AI-ECG triage thresholds for early rule-out and rule-in of AMI were also evaluated.
Findings: Among 12,630 patients with an available digital 12-lead ECG (5047 in APACE and 7583 in APACE-Light), adjudicated AMI was diagnosed in 19% (968/5047) and 18% (1386/7583) of patients, respectively. In patients with hs-cTnT at presentation (n = 5031 and n = 7565), the AI-ECG model showed good diagnostic performance for AMI with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.78 (95% CI: 0.77-0.80) and 0.84 (0.83-0.85) and an area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) of 0.56 (0.53-0.59) and 0.65 (0.62-0.67). Its discrimination was inferior to hs-cTnT (AUC 0.94 [0.93-0.95] and 0.93 [0.92-0.94]). The AI-ECG model provided some incremental diagnostic value when combined with hs-cTnT (AUC 0.95 [0.94-0.96] and 0.95 [0.94-0.95], p < 0.001). The predefined triage thresholds ruled out 14% (706/5031) and 19% (1437/7565) of patients, with a sensitivity for AMI of 97.6% (96.5-98.5) and 97.5% (96.6-98.3), respectively.
Interpretation: AI-ECG showed high, but not very high, diagnostic accuracy for AMI. As a diagnosis of AMI is unlikely to be ruled out on ECG alone, combining AI-ECG with hs-cTnT may improve decision making in the ED, warranting prospective studies.
Funding: The Swiss National Science Foundation, the Swiss Heart Foundation, Innosuisse, the University Hospital Basel, the University of Basel, Abbott, Beckman Coulter, Idorsia, LSI Medience Corporation, Roche, Ortho Clinical Diagnostics, Quidel, Siemens, SpinChip, Upstream, and Singulex, the Korea Health Industry Development Institute (KHIDI), funded by the Ministry of Health & Welfare, Republic of Korea (grant number: RS-2026-25543703).

paper.title: A decentralized federated learning approach for predicting chemoradiotherapy response from multicenter whole-slide images.
paper.abstract:
Purpose: Given the institutional and regulatory barriers to centralized sharing of multicenter whole-slide image (WSI) data for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model development without requiring centralized sharing raw WSI data. This study explores a WSI-based FL model for predicting chemoradiotherapy response in advanced NSCLC, and compares its performance with centralized deep learning (DL) and clinical models using external multi-center validation cohorts.
Methods: This study collected WSI and corresponding clinical data from 250 patients across four hospitals. We developed a centralized DL model and a FL model based on WSI, with patch-level predictions aggregated to patient-level outcomes using a voting method. In addition, we built a clinical logistic regression model using clinical data. All models were evaluated on two independent external cohorts (Hospital C and Hospital D). Performance was summarized as the mean and 95% confidence interval across the five models obtained from five-fold cross-validation.
Results: Across both external validation cohorts, WSI-based models consistently outperformed the clinical model. The FL model achieved performance comparable to the DL model. In hospital C, the DL model had an accuracy/AUC of 0.68/0.64, while the FL model achieved 0.70/0.65. The clinical model had an accuracy/AUC of 0.58/0.58. In hospital D, the DL model had an accuracy/AUC of 0.68/0.68, while the FL model achieved 0.73/0.71. The clinical model had an accuracy/AUC of 0.61/0.59.
Conclusion: The FL model using WSI achieved performance comparable to the centralized DL model in predicting NSCLC outcomes, while allowing each participating institution to retain its local data. It also showed consistent performance across independent external validation cohorts. This approach provides a practical solution for collaborative model development in multi-center pathology studies, particularly in settings where data sharing is restricted.

paper.title: Development and external validation of an explainable machine-learning model for the prediction of unfavourable clinical-radiological outcome at three months in thoracolumbar osteoporotic vertebral fractures.
paper.abstract:
Unlabelled: No externally validated tools stratify three-month prognosis after thoracolumbar osteoporotic vertebral fracture. An explainable logistic-regression model with nine predictors achieved an external AUC-ROC of 0.744 (sensitivity 90.7%). The counterfactual analysis of vertebral augmentation, the only modifiable predictor, is hypothesis-generating and should not be interpreted as a treatment recommendation.
Purpose: Thoracolumbar osteoporotic vertebral fractures (OVF) carry substantial morbidity and mortality, yet no externally validated tool stratifies three-month prognosis. We developed and externally validated an explainable machine-learning model for the three-month unfavourable clinical-radiological outcome.
Methods: Retrospective observational study reported according to TRIPOD. Unfavourable outcome was defined as persistent pain, progression of vertebral height loss and/or worsening of independence in daily activities. A derivation cohort of 482 patients aged ≥50 years with acute thoracolumbar OVF treated at a tertiary centre (2017-2021) was used to train and internally validate seven algorithms with hyperparameter optimisation and stratified fivefold cross-validation. An independent two-centre cohort (n = 74) was used for external validation without retraining. Interpretability was based on SHAP values.
Results: The unfavourable outcome occurred in 53.9% of the derivation cohort and 58.1% of the external cohort. A nine-variable logistic-regression model with Platt calibration was selected (cross-validated AUC-ROC 0.675, 95% CI 0.622-0.728; external AUC-ROC 0.744, 95% CI 0.628-0.844). At the pre-specified internal Youden threshold (0.556), external sensitivity was 60.5% and specificity 71.0%; at a post-hoc external threshold (0.432), 90.7% and 54.8% (Brier 0.211, expected calibration error 0.096). Vertebral augmentation was the strongest and only modifiable predictor (mean |SHAP | = 0.278); counterfactual analysis showed an absolute risk reduction of 17.1-26.6 percentage points (median 25.3).
Conclusion: The model predicts the three-month outcome of thoracolumbar OVF with an external AUC-ROC of 0.744 and preserved calibration. The counterfactual analysis of vertebral augmentation is hypothesis-generating and not a treatment recommendation; larger external validation, long-term outcomes and harm assessment are required before clinical use.

paper.title: MedReShaper: mesh-based AI for 3D anatomical shape completion in orbital fracture reconstruction with controlled technical validation.
paper.abstract: Accurate three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction of missing orbital anatomy is important for surgical planning and patient-specific implant (PSI) design. Existing approaches often rely on contralateral mirroring or statistical shape priors, which may be limited in bilateral or anatomically asymmetric cases. We introduce MedReShaper, a mesh-based AI method for direct unilateral orbital reconstruction from incomplete 3D surfaces using only preserved ipsilateral anatomical information. MedReShaper integrates anatomy-guided multi-view projections, ASC-Net, and multi-angle candidate refinement to reconstruct missing orbital geometry directly from incomplete meshes. The model was developed using 2,400 health unilateral orbital meshes from UZ Leuven and evaluated in three stages: controlled technical validation on 120 independent cases with intact orbital anatomy with virtual defects, multicenter external technical validation on 1,187 external cases with intact orbital anatomy from 12 external cohorts from multiple institutions and data sources using the same controlled-defect strategy, and retrospective clinical evaluation on 45 patients with genuine traumatic orbital fractures using expert-derived reference surfaces and independent surgeon assessment. In Stage I, mean point-cloud and surface errors were 0.46 ± 0.32 mm and 0.57 ± 0.38 mm, respectively. Broadly consistent performance was maintained across the Stage II external cohort, with mean center-level errors of 0.49 mm and 0.60 mm. In Stage III, MedReShaper achieved a full-surface error of 0.61 ± 0.43 mm and a mean reconstruction time of 54.1 ± 15.7 s per case, demonstrating competitive geometric accuracy with favorable clinical usability and reconstruction efficiency. These results demonstrate robust technical performance across independent and multicenter datasets and provide initial clinical evidence supporting further evaluation of MedReShaper for orbital fracture reconstruction and surgical planning.

paper.title: Development and validation of an ML-driven risk prediction model for stroke-heart syndrome after acute ischemic stroke.
paper.abstract:
Background: Existing prediction models for stroke-heart syndrome (SHS) after acute ischemic stroke (AIS) have limited generalizability due to population heterogeneity.
Objective: To develop and validate a generalizable risk prediction model for SHS following AIS.
Methods: A retrospective cohort of 1404 AIS patients from the MIMIC-IV database was utilized. After feature selection, 14 machine learning algorithms were evaluated. All algorithms were trained under identical preprocessing with per-algorithm automatically tuned hyperparameters and evaluated by five-fold cross-validation and hold-out internal validation. The final model-a logistic regression-based nomogram-was externally validated on an independent single-center cohort (n = 321). Performance was assessed by discrimination (area under the curve [AUC]), calibration (calibration curves, Hosmer-Lemeshow test), and clinical utility (decision curve analysis). Model interpretability was augmented using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP).
Results: Seven early-admission predictors were identified: age, heart rate, prothrombin time, blood urea nitrogen, Glasgow Coma Scale score, respiratory rate, and body temperature. The model demonstrated strong, consistent discrimination across datasets: training AUC=0.789, internal validation AUC=0.802, and external validation AUC=0.810. Calibration was good on internal validation (Hosmer-Lemeshow P = 0.614) but showed external under-dispersion (slope 1.72, P = 0.004); local recalibration is indicated. Decision curve analysis confirmed clinical net benefit across a range of threshold probabilities.
Conclusion: We developed and validated a parsimonious SHS risk prediction model using seven early-admission indicators that overcomes the generalizability limitations of prior tools through multi-algorithm validation and external testing. Relying on routine clinical variables, this tool facilitates rapid risk stratification for precision prevention, though future prospective validation in diverse populations is warranted.

paper.title: MRI Radiomics and Deep Learning for Differentiating Spinal Tuberculosis from Spinal Metastasis: A Multicenter Study.
paper.abstract:
Objectives: To develop radiomics model, 2D deep learning (2D DL) model, 2.5D deep learning (2.5D DL) model, 3D deep learning (3D DL) model, and their fusion models to differentiate spinal tuberculosis (STB) from spinal metastasis (SM) based on MR imaging.
Methods: This retrospective study included 186 STB patients and 219 SM patients. Patients from three hospitals were divided into a training set (n = 191), an internal test set (n = 82) and an external test set (n = 132). Using the ResNet50 network pre-trained leveraging the ImageNet dataset, we developed 2D, 2.5D, and 3D deep learning models based on MR imaging. We constructed the radiomics model by using PyRadiomics to extract radiomics features. Deep learning models and radiomics model were used to construct two fusion models: the feature-based model (Rad_DL_FB) and the decision-based model (Rad_DL_DB). And the accuracy of these models was validated.
Results: In the internal test set, the Rad_DL_FB model demonstrated superior performance compared to other models, achieving the highest AUC of 0.971 (95% CI: 0.953-0.989) and accuracy of 0.927. In the external test set, the Rad_DL_DB model demonstrated superior performance compared to other models, achieving the highest AUC of 0.961 (95% CI: 0.940-0.982) and accuracy of 0.909. Furthermore, fusion-model assistance significantly improved the diagnostic accuracy of junior spine surgeons and narrowed the observed performance gap between junior and senior surgeons.
Conclusion: The fusion models including Rad_DL_FB model and Rad_DL_DB model, which integrates radiomics features and deep learning features of different dimensions, can effectively differentiate STB from SM, thereby assisting clinicians in making clinical decisions.

paper.title: Development of Prediction Model of Diabetes Self-Management Core Behaviours Based on Deep Learning.
paper.abstract:
Aims: This study aimed to develop a predictive model for diabetes self-management (DSM) using a fully connected neural network (FCNN) architecture. The model's performance was rigorously evaluated using key metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC).
Design: A quantitative, multicenter cross-sectional design.
Methods: A systematic literature review identified key psychosocial factors and corresponding validated scales, which formed the initial item pool. A multicenter cross-sectional study was then conducted to collect data on these items from 2005 participants across five research centers in Hainan, Zhejiang, Jiangsu, and Henan provinces. We chose to develop an FCNN model over traditional approaches including logistic regression and random forest, as it could automatically capture complex, non-linear relationships among predictors without manual feature engineering. Using this model for gradient-based feature importance ranking, we selected the most predictive items from the initial pool following preliminary screening of overlapping items. After feature selection, the model was retrained using the selected features, with 80% of the data allocated for training and 20% for testing. Finally, model performance was validated through a two-week prospective observational study.
Results: Twenty-four out of 99 candidate variables were identified as model characteristics for predicting DSM behaviours. The model demonstrated strong performance across all four self-management domains. For healthy eating, the accuracy, precision, recall, and AUC were 83.34%, 88.56%, 90.05%, and 0.84%, respectively. For medication adherence, these values were 82.14%, 86.60%, 90.27%, and 0.84%, respectively. For regular exercise, they were 82.39%, 82.89%, 86.09%, and 0.89%, respectively. For blood glucose monitoring, they were 83.39%, 85.45%, 89.72%, and 0.87%, respectively. The prospective validation cohort (n = 50) further confirmed the model's robust performance, yielding AUCs of 0.84, 0.82, 0.83, and 0.89 for diet, exercise, blood glucose monitoring, and medication adherence, respectively.
Conclusion: The FCNN-based predictive model demonstrated promising performance in forecasting DSM behaviours, with particularly strong discriminative ability as evidenced by high accuracy and AUC values. These findings suggest that deep learning approaches incorporating psychosocial and clinical variables may help predict DSM behaviours, although the model requires further validation before it can be considered a clinical tool for personalized diabetes care. Although the prospective validation results are encouraging, they should be interpreted as preliminary given the limited sample size (n = 50); larger-scale, multicenter external validation studies are warranted to further confirm the model's generalizability and clinical applicability.
Impact: Predicting core diabetes self-management behaviours using an FCNN may provide useful insights into individualized adherence patterns and could inform targeted, stepped-care interventions, although further validation is needed before clinical application.
Reporting Method: The reporting of this cross-sectional study followed the STROBE guideline.
Patient Or Public Contribution: Patients with Type 2 diabetes mellitus contributed to this study by completing questionnaires during the model development phase (n = 2005) and by participating in the prospective validation phase (n = 50). No patients or public members were involved in study design, data analysis, or interpretation of results. Study findings will be disseminated to participants through their respective endocrinology departments.

paper.title: Mode-specific fetal heart rate signal dropout as a marker of perinatal asphyxia: A multicenter observational study using causal machine learning methods.
paper.abstract:
Objective: Cardiotocography (CTG) is the standard method for intrapartum fetal monitoring. Modern systems acquire fetal heart rate (FHR) using external Doppler ultrasound (US) or internal fetal scalp electrocardiography (ECG). We evaluated whether mode-specific FHR signal dropout was associated with perinatal asphyxia and whether it should be retained as an informative, mode-aware feature for downstream predictive models.
Methods: We conducted a retrospective multicenter cohort study using routinely collected clinical and CTG data from Mercy Hospital for Women, Melbourne, Australia, for 2010-2021; Werribee Mercy Hospital, Melbourne, Australia, for 2010-2021; and the Czech CTU-UHB database from University Hospital Brno, for 2010-2012. A total of 46 662 labor episodes at ≥36 weeks' gestation with ≥15 min of interpretable CTG data in the final 60 min before birth were analyzed (32 242 in the model-development cohort, 548 in the Czech validation cohort, and 13 872 in the Australian community validation cohort). The exposure was mode-specific FHR dropout, classified as US low dropout, US high dropout (>30%), ECG low dropout, or ECG high dropout (>30%). The primary outcome was sustained perinatal asphyxia, defined using a Delphi-consensus composite of clinical, biochemical, and neurologic criteria.
Results: In the model-development cohort, 860 cases of perinatal asphyxia occurred (2.67%, 95% CI 2.49%-2.85%). Compared with US low dropout, ECG high dropout was associated with higher risk of asphyxia (inverse probability weighting IPW-adjusted odds ratio [OR] 3.14, 95% CI 2.20-4.48; targeted maximum likelihood estimation-adjusted OR 2.08, 95% CI 1.21-3.58), corresponding to an absolute risk increase of 2.27% (one additional case per 44 births). Survival analysis supported elevated hazards (HR 4.76, 95% CI 2.98-7.62). External validation supported the direction of association, although estimates varied across cohorts.
Conclusion: In retrospective multicenter analyses, high FHR dropout during ECG monitoring was associated with increased perinatal asphyxia risk. These findings support evaluating mode-specific dropout as an informative signal-quality feature in future predictive models. Prospective validation of such models is needed before clinical implementation.

paper.title: Continuous prediction of prolonged intensive care unit stay from longitudinal electronic health record data: development and external validation.
paper.abstract:
Objectives: To develop and externally validate Prognostic Estimator of RiSk for prolonged ICU STay (PERSIST), a model that continuously updates the probability of an intensive care unit (ICU) stay longer than 7 days during the first week of ICU admission.
Materials And Methods: We developed PERSIST, an XGBoost model, on 49 255 adult ICU stays from the Mount Sinai Health System (MSHS; 2021-2025) and externally validated it in 72 156 Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care-IV (MIMIC-IV) stays (2008-2019). Sixty routinely available electronic health record (EHR) features were aggregated hourly, with predictions every 4 hours from preceding data, benchmarked against L2-regularized logistic regression. We assessed discrimination, calibration, net benefit, SHapley Additive exPlanations attributions, and subgroup performance.
Results: Prolonged stay occurred in 16.1% of MSHS and 11.1% of MIMIC-IV admissions. PERSIST achieved macroaveraged areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.80 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.79-0.81) and 0.78 (0.77-0.78), respectively, compared with 0.75 (0.73-0.76) and 0.74 (0.73-0.74) for logistic regression. Corresponding areas under the precision-recall curve were 0.73 and 0.68. Brier scores were 0.14 and 0.13. Across modeled thresholds, PERSIST provided greater net benefit than treat-all and treat-none strategies. Discrimination was similar across reported age, sex, and racial groups.
Discussion: Prognostic Estimator of RiSk for prolonged ICU STay transported across 2 health systems differing in era, case mix, and outcome prevalence, and outperformed logistic regression under identical conditions. Net benefit was greatest during the early ICU days, when few patients have declared a prolonged trajectory and a risk estimate can still inform planning.
Conclusion: Continuously updated, EHR-based prediction of prolonged ICU stay is feasible and generalizable. Prospective evaluation should determine whether it improves ICU care coordination and capacity planning.

paper.title: Multi-scale convolution with efficient channel attention improves benign-malignant classification of spinal tumors on T2-weighted fat-suppressed MRI.
paper.abstract:
Background: Accurate differentiation between benign and malignant spinal tumors is critical for treatment planning, yet manual interpretation of T2-weighted fat-suppressed MRI remains subjective, with substantial inter-observer variability. This study aimed to develop a deep learning model, the multi-scale deep residual network (MSDR-Net), for automated benign-malignant classification.
Methods: A total of 500 T2-weighted fat-suppressed MR images of pathologically confirmed spinal tumors (389 benign, 111 malignant) were retrospectively collected from two institutions. Data were partitioned into training (70%), validation (20%), and independent test (10%) sets, and five-fold cross-validation was performed. Leave-one-center-out external validation was also performed (development: Institution A, n = 300; evaluation: Institution B, n = 200). The proposed MSDR-Net incorporates multi-branch residual blocks that combine parallel multi-scale convolutional paths with efficient channel attention modules and was benchmarked against six established architectures.
Results: On the independent test set (N = 50; 12 malignant cases), MSDR-Net achieved 92.0% accuracy, 91.7% sensitivity (95% CI 61.5%-99.8%), 92.1% specificity, and an AUC of 0.921, the highest point estimates among evaluated architectures. The model was well calibrated (Brier score 0.072), with net benefit over treat-all strategies across thresholds of 0.10-0.60. Derived from a small test cohort, these estimates carry substantial uncertainty and await confirmation in larger, prospective cohorts. External-cohort accuracy was 86.5% (AUC 0.875). Ablation experiments showed that removing either component degraded performance, with a modest super-additive interaction; given their substantially smaller capacity, the single-path variants' deficit cannot be attributed solely to removing multi-scale processing. The model has 55.4M parameters and 12.3-ms inference per image.
Conclusion: MSDR-Net effectively captures multi-scale discriminative features of spinal tumors on T2-weighted fat-suppressed MRI, achieving high classification accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency. The model shows promise for clinical deployment as an auxiliary diagnostic tool for orthopedic surgeons and radiologists.

paper.title: Multimodal CT radiomics and 2.5D deep learning for preoperative grading of clear cell renal cell carcinoma in older patients: a multicenter study.
paper.abstract:
Introduction: To develop and validate a multimodal CT-based model integrating intra-peritumoral radiomics, 2.5D deep learning (DL), and clinical-radiological features for preoperative prediction of World Health Organization/International Society of Urological Pathology (WHO/ISUP) grade in older patients with clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC).
Methods: This multicenter retrospective study included 1,103 patients older than 60 years with pathologically confirmed ccRCC from four hospitals. Patients were allocated to a training cohort (n=459), an internal validation cohort (n=198), and two independent external test cohorts (test1, n=227; test2, n=219). WHO/ISUP grades I-II were classified as low grade and grades III-IV as high grade. Radiomics features were extracted from corticomedullary-phase CT images using intratumoral and progressively expanded intra-peritumoral regions of 1, 2, and 3 mm. In parallel, 2D and 2.5D DL features were extracted using ImageNet-pretrained ResNet34 networks, with the 2.5D approach integrating axial, coronal, and sagittal tumor views. After feature selection, five machine learning classifiers were evaluated. The optimal radiomics model, DL model, and clinical model were integrated using stacking-based decision-level fusion. Model performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic analysis, calibration curves, decision curve analysis (DCA), and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP).
Results: The random forest (RF) model based on intra-peritumoral 3-mm radiomics features achieved areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUCs) of 0.754 (95% CI, 0.683-0.825) and 0.725 (95% CI, 0.655-0.794) in the test1 and test2 cohorts, respectively. The RF model based on 2.5D DL features achieved corresponding AUCs of 0.756 (95% CI, 0.682-0.830) and 0.713 (95% CI, 0.643-0.783). The multimodal combined model achieved numerically higher external AUCs than the selected single-modality models, reaching 0.775 (95% CI, 0.705-0.845) in test1 and 0.732 (95% CI, 0.664-0.800) in test2. DCA demonstrated favorable clinical net benefit for the combined model, while SHAP analysis identified the 2.5D DL component as the largest contributor to model predictions.
Discussion: A multimodal CT-based framework integrating intra-peritumoral radiomics, 2.5D DL, and clinical-radiological information enabled noninvasive preoperative prediction of WHO/ISUP grade in older patients with ccRCC and maintained predictive performance across independent external cohorts. This approach may provide complementary imaging and clinical information for preoperative risk stratification and individualized treatment planning.

paper.title: Development and validation of a risk stratification model for mild cognitive impairment among older adults with possible sarcopenia integrating traditional Chinese medicine constitution: a multicenter cross-sectional study.
paper.abstract:
Background: Possible sarcopenia is associated with cognitive impairment among older adults, while mild cognitive impairment (MCI) represents an important window for early identification. Existing MCI assessment approaches may depend on neuroimaging, genetic testing, or biochemical biomarkers, limiting their use in large-scale screening. Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) constitution may provide accessible information on individual physiological and functional characteristics, but it has rarely been incorporated into MCI risk stratification.
Objective: To develop and validate a machine learning-based risk stratification model integrating TCM constitution and conventional health-related indicators for MCI among older adults with possible sarcopenia.
Methods: This multicenter cross-sectional study included 3,310 older adults with possible sarcopenia from ten tertiary hospitals in China and an independent single-institution external validation sample of 314 participants. The concurrent outcome was screening-defined probable MCI based on a prespecified Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) criterion. After a stratified 7:3 training-internal-validation split, data-dependent preprocessing parameters and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) feature selection were estimated using the training data only. Multilayer perceptron (MLP), gradient boosting decision tree (GBDT), support vector machine, K-nearest neighbors, logistic regression, and AdaBoost models were fitted using prespecified settings and evaluated using discrimination, classification, calibration, and decision-curve measures. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) were used only to describe contributions to model output.
Results: Seven features were retained: educational attainment, sex, smartphone usage, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index score, Patient Health Questionnaire-9 score, qi-deficiency constitution, and damp-heat constitution. The MLP showed the highest internal discrimination, with an AUC of 0.853 (95% CI: 0.827-0.878); its AUC was 0.799 (95% CI: 0.773-0.823) in the external sample. The internal and external Brier scores were 0.168 and 0.151, calibration intercepts were -0.07 and 0.18, and calibration slopes were 0.80 and 1.07, respectively. SHAP analysis ranked feature contributions to model output and was not interpreted causally.
Conclusion: This cross-sectional screening framework integrated TCM constitution with conventional indicators to stratify the probability of current screening-defined probable MCI among older adults with possible sarcopenia. The single-institution external evaluation supports only limited transportability; prospective multicenter evaluation and, where needed, recalibration are required before clinical implementation.

paper.title: Classification Performance of a Deep Learning Algorithm for Common Skin Lesions in the Emergency Department: A Multicenter Preliminary Validation Study.
paper.abstract: Background/Objectives: Initial classification of skin lesions in the emergency department (ED) is difficult when dermatology consultations are limited. This study externally validated a deep learning (DL) algorithm for classifying three common ED skin lesions and explored whether algorithmic pre-classification was associated with changes in the classification performance of medical staff. Methods: A ResNet-50-based algorithm was developed using 6000 clinical images from 4815 patients. For external validation, 100 images from an independent institution were classified by the algorithm and nine medical staff members (three emergency medicine specialists, three residents, and three physician assistant [PA] nurses). Fifteen days later, the staff reclassified the same randomly reordered images with the algorithmic pre-classification provided. Results: In external validation, the algorithm showed an overall accuracy of 0.96 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.90-0.99), lesion-specific balanced accuracies of 0.95-0.96, and a macro-average area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.98 (95% CI, 0.95-1.00). Unassisted, the three PA nurses differed significantly from the algorithm for urticaria and herpes zoster (all p < 0.01, McNemar's exact test). After receiving algorithmic assistance, all medical staff showed a balanced accuracy of 0.97 or higher for all three lesions. In the mixed-effects model, assistance was associated with higher odds of correct classification (odds ratio 25.9, 95% CI 11.7-57.2), and inter-rater agreement (Fleiss' κ) increased from 0.70 to 0.97. Conclusions: The algorithm demonstrated high classification performance on independent external validation, and algorithmic assistance was associated with improved classification performance, with the largest absolute gains among medical staff with lower unassisted accuracy. As these findings are exploratory, they should be confirmed in randomized prospective studies.

paper.title: An Interpretable Multimodal Model Integrating Multiparametric MRI Radiomics and Body Composition for Preoperative Risk Stratification of Malignant Transformation in Rectal Adenomas: A Two-Center Study.
paper.abstract:
Background/Objectives: Preoperative identification of malignant transformation in rectal adenomas (RAs) is challenging because endoscopic biopsy may not sample focal malignant components. This study aimed to develop and externally validate an interpretable multimodal model for preoperative risk stratification of malignant transformation in RAs.
Methods: In this retrospective two-center study, 359 surgically treated patients were allocated to training (n = 143), internal validation (n = 61), and external validation (n = 155) cohorts. Radiomic features derived from high-resolution T2-weighted imaging (HRT2WI) and diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), clinical biomarkers, and CT-derived body composition metrics were evaluated. Five machine learning algorithms were compared for each radiomics signature. The final combined logistic regression model integrated the selected HRT2WI and DWI radiomics model-predicted probabilities with clinical and body composition predictors. Discrimination, calibration, and decision curve analyses were performed.
Results: The malignant transformation was present in 65/143 patients (45.5%) in the training cohort and 91/155 (58.7%) in the external cohort, a difference of 13.3 percentage points. The combined model achieved area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) values of 0.956 (95% CI, 0.922-0.981), 0.908 (95% CI, 0.830-0.970), and 0.867 (95% CI, 0.803-0.919) in the training, internal validation, and external validation cohorts, respectively. In external validation, the combined model outperformed the four component models and the junior radiologist (all p < 0.05); its performance did not differ significantly from that of the senior radiologist (p = 0.093). Note that this reader comparison included only one junior and one senior radiologist and is exploratory and cannot support general conclusions regarding model performance versus radiologists in broader clinical practice. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis identified the visceral-to-subcutaneous fat ratio (VSR), DWI radiomics model-predicted probability, and the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) as the leading contributors to the combined model.
Conclusions: This interpretable two-center model showed promising discrimination for preoperative risk stratification of malignant transformation in surgically treated RAs. It may help identify patients who warrant further preoperative assessment or multidisciplinary discussion. Prospective multicenter evaluation is required before clinical implementation.

paper.title: Real-Time Machine Learning Model to Predict Cardiac Arrest Within 12 Hours in Critically Ill Patients (DeepiCARS): A Confirmatory Trial and External Validation.
paper.abstract: Background/Objectives: Continuous prediction of cardiac arrest in the intensive care unit (ICU) must be judged by considering alarm burden as well as discrimination. We evaluated DeepiCARS (iCARS), an approved recurrent-network and gradient-boosting ensemble, developed at one centre and temporally validated there, predicting in-ICU cardiac arrest within 12 h. Methods: The unchanged model was assessed in a retrospective 1:1 matched confirmatory trial at that centre (214 adults, 107 with arrest), which assigned no intervention and required no registration, and in 30,487 adult ICU admissions at an independent Korean tertiary centre (2010-2021; 2782 with an in-window arrest: 653 with cardiopulmonary resuscitation [CPR] and 2129 deaths without CPR), against seven conventional scores, per subject in the trial and per prediction point externally, on discrimination, sensitivity at matched alarm burden, lead time and calibration. Results: The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) with the extended input (vital signs, Glasgow Coma Scale, age, sex and 21 laboratory values) was 0.9428 (95% confidence interval 0.9102-0.9753) in the trial and 0.9587 (0.9548-0.9626) externally, and with the core (non-laboratory) input 0.9103 (0.8716-0.9490) and 0.9458 (0.9415-0.9500), above every comparator. For arrests with CPR, the external AUROC was 0.8697 (0.8538-0.8854) with the extended input and 0.8425 (0.8264-0.8591) with the core input, above the National Early Warning Score 2 (NEWS2), 0.7157 (0.6987-0.7319), and the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA), 0.7424 (0.7205-0.7631). At no greater alarm burden than NEWS2 ≥ 7 and SOFA ≥ 11, iCARS with the extended input detected 37.17 (35.75-38.65) and 30.66 (28.76-32.65) percentage points more of the points preceding an arrest, with median lead times within the 12 h window of 11.42 h and 11.50 h; the score was already above threshold when the window opened in 53.8% and 58.3% of admissions with an arrest, and first crossed it a median of 72.42 h and 80.84 h before the arrest. Conclusions: Evaluated unchanged, the approved model retained high discrimination externally, including for arrests with CPR, and detected more of the points preceding an arrest than conventional scores at no greater alarm burden. No operating threshold is proposed.

paper.title: A Modular Diabetic Retinopathy Analysis Framework for Lesion Segmentation and Severity Grading: Cross-Dataset External Validation from APTOS to Messidor-2.
paper.abstract: Background/Objectives: High in-domain accuracy of diabetic retinopathy (DR) grading models does not guarantee a similar performance for a new population. We quantify how an APTOS-trained grader degrades on an independent cohort and examine why. Methods: A modular framework combines a ResNet-34 U-Net for lesion segmentation (IDRiD) with an EfficientNet-B0 severity grader (APTOS 2019), optionally fused with lesion-derived and frequency features. The grader was evaluated zero-shot on Messidor-2 (n=1744) with bootstrap confidence intervals, four training seeds, referable-DR analysis, a discrimination-versus-calibration decomposition, a paired preprocessing ablation, and a duplicate audit. Results: Quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) fell from 0.873 (95% CI 0.831-0.909) on the APTOS test set to 0.455 (0.400-0.507) on Messidor-2; across four seeds the external QWK was 0.410±0.057. Referable-DR sensitivity fell from 92.7% to 35.0% (specificity 93.9% and 96.6%) and the AUC from 0.984 to 0.795, indicating both a loss of discrimination and a calibration shift; recalibrating thresholds with target labels (cross-validated) raised QWK only to 0.583. Omitting CLAHE reduced QWK to 0.326 (paired difference 0.129, 0.089-0.171). Thirty-three APTOS test images duplicated in the training or validation data changed QWK marginally (0.866). Lesion-feature fusion did not significantly improve grading. The segmentation Dice on lesion-containing patches was 0.51-0.68, whereas the per-image Dice was 0.21-0.61. Conclusions: In-domain agreement is a poor proxy for external performance; multi-seed reporting, explicit calibration analysis, and preprocessing control are needed before clinical use.

paper.title: Decoding the Prognosis of Sepsis-Induced Acute Lung Injury: Machine Learning Model Development and SHAP Interpretability Analysis Based on Critical Care Databases.
paper.abstract: Background: Sepsis-induced acute lung injury (SI-ALI) has high morbidity and mortality. Early prognosis prediction is critical, but traditional scoring systems lack dynamic, interpretable, and personalized capabilities. This study aimed to develop and validate an interpretable machine learning model for predicting mortality in SI-ALI. Methods: Data from the MIMIC-IV database (training/internal validation) and from the eICU-CRD database (external validation) were analyzed. The Lasso regression model with cross-validation was utilized for the identification of the key features. Subsequently, a series of predicted models were formulated utilizing six distinct machine learning algorithms, and the performance of the models was evaluated using various analytical tools. SHAP values were employed to interpret the machine learning models. Results: Among 7250 patients, eight key indicators were identified. The GBDT model achieved an internal AUC of 0.801 (95% CI: 0.775-0.827), accuracy 0.730, sensitivity 0.692, and specificity 0.739. External validation showed an AUC of 0.681 (95% CI: 0.650-0.708), accuracy 0.601, sensitivity 0.686, and specificity 0.574. However, precision, F1, and MCC were modest, indicating limited predictive accuracy. SHAP identified urine output, respiratory rate, BUN, PLR, lactate, INR, age, and anion gap as the most influential variables. Conclusions: The GBDT model showed modest discriminative ability and limited generalizability. It should be considered an exploratory tool requiring further prospective multicenter validation before clinical application.

paper.title: Synchronous Differentiated Thyroid Carcinoma in Non-Invasive Follicular Thyroid Neoplasm with Papillary-like Nuclear Features (NIFTP): Prevalence, Pathological Profile, and Limits of Pre-Operative Risk Prediction in a Multicentre Cohort.
paper.abstract: Background/Objectives: Non-invasive follicular thyroid neoplasm with papillary-like nuclear features (NIFTP) was reclassified as a non-malignant entity in 2016 to reduce overtreatment. A proportion of NIFTP-containing glands nonetheless harbour a synchronous differentiated thyroid carcinoma (DTC). We quantified its prevalence and pathological profile and assessed whether routinely collected pre-operative variables identify affected patients. Methods: A multicentre retrospective cohort of 1185 adults with NIFTP confirmed at second histological review, operated on between 2017 and 2023 in 22 centres. The outcome was a synchronous DTC in the surgical specimen. A weighted random forest and an elastic-net logistic regression based on 13 pre-operative predictors were evaluated with 20-times repeated five-fold cross-validation, with all data-driven steps nested within training folds, and with leave-one-centre-out and temporal validation. Results: A synchronous DTC was present in 61 patients (5.1%; 95% CI 4.0-6.6; 6.2% after review of the stored reports), with marked between-centre variation (none recorded in eight centres). Fifty-eight carcinomas (95%) were pT1a; none had gross extra-thyroidal extension or nodal metastasis (nodes examined in 27 patients), and none met the 2025 American Thyroid Association criteria mandating a more extensive operation. No pre-operative variable differed between groups after multiplicity adjustment. The cross-validated AUROC was 0.56 (95% CI 0.47-0.65) for the random forest and 0.58 (0.48-0.67) for the elastic net; the within-centre concordance was 0.48 and the temporal-validation AUROC 0.39, and decision-curve analysis showed no net benefit over default strategies. Conclusions: About one in twenty NIFTP-containing specimens harbours a synchronous DTC, usually a low-risk papillary microcarcinoma. Routinely available pre-operative variables do not identify these patients; management should be guided by the pathology of the carcinoma itself.

paper.title: Development and validation of a simplified two-point sampling strategy for predicting in-hospital mortality in elderly ICU sepsis patients: a multicenter retrospective cohort study.
paper.abstract:
Background: Sepsis is a leading cause of death in the intensive care unit (ICU), with significantly higher rates in elderly patients due to immunosenescence and greater comorbidity burden. Existing machine learning models for ICU mortality prediction predominantly rely on fixed-time-window feature extraction without evaluating how temporal sampling density influences performance. This study aimed to compare the effects of different temporal sampling density strategies on in-hospital mortality prediction in elderly sepsis patients and identify the sampling density beyond which additional measurements provide limited incremental value.
Methods: This retrospective cohort study used the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV database as the development set and the Electronic ICU Collaborative Research Database as the external validation set. Patients aged 65 years or older who met the Sepsis-3 criteria and had an ICU stay of at least 24 h were included. A fixed-architecture long short-term memory network was used to compare six temporal sampling strategies (1-point, 2-point, 3-point, 4-point, 6-point, and 24-point) under a unified feature set and training strategy. Model performance was evaluated in terms of the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, the area under the precision-recall curve, the F1 score, and the Brier score. Interpretability analysis was performed to identify the leading predictive features of the best-performing model.
Results: Of the 546,028 screened records, 20,163 elderly sepsis patients were included. The 2-point group (admission and 23-hour) achieved the highest discrimination (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.814, 95% confidence interval 0.809-0.818), with the largest improvement over the single-point group (0.122; P < 0.001). The difference versus the 24-point hourly group was not statistically significant (P = 0.961), indicating comparable discrimination between the two strategies. Adding intermediate sampling points beyond 2 points yielded no additional gain. Sensitivity analysis indicated that the 23-hour endpoint contains richer prognostic information than earlier timepoints do. External validation (n = 11,039) supported these findings. The 23-hour Glasgow Coma Scale score, blood urea nitrogen, and lactate level were the core predictive indicators.
Conclusions: In elderly ICU sepsis patients, a simplified two-point sampling strategy (admission baseline and 23-hour endpoint) achieves discrimination comparable to that of hourly dense monitoring. Intermediate sampling points provide no additional gain, suggesting that simplified sampling is sufficient under ICU data sparsity constraints.

paper.title: Impact of Image Bit Depth Reduction on Deep Learning Performance in Chest Radiograph Analysis: A Multi-institutional Study.
paper.abstract:
Rationale And Objectives: Medical imaging typically generates 12-bit to 16-bit formats, yet conversion to 8-bit is often required. While deep learning has been widely explored in medical imaging, the influence of image bit depth on model performance is not fully understood. This study evaluates the impact of conversion from 16-bit to 8-bit for sex, age, and obesity classification using deep learning.
Materials And Methods: In this retrospective, multi-institutional study, we analyzed 100,002 chest radiographs from 48,047 participants across three institutions. Images were uniformly quantized from the fixed 0-65535 range to 256 levels (0-255) with no additional processing. Three convolutional neural network architectures (ResNet52, EfficientNetB2, and ConvNeXtSmall) were trained on both 16-bit and 8-bit versions of the images. Model performance was evaluated using internal test datasets, randomly split multiple times, and an external test dataset. Statistical analysis included paired comparisons of area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC) values, with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons.
Results: Across all architectures and classification tasks, differences between 16-bit and 8-bit model performance were minimal (mean differences ranging from -0.218%-0.184%). Statistical analyses revealed no significant differences in AUC-ROC values between bit depths for any model-task combination (all p values > 0.05 after Bonferroni correction). Effect sizes were small to moderate (Cohen's d ranging from -0.415-0.391).
Conclusion: No statistically significant differences were detected between models trained on 16-bit and 8-bit images in the three evaluated tasks. These findings suggest that conversion to 8-bit images may reduce data storage requirements and improve data processing efficiency. Further research is needed to assess their usefulness in clinical tasks.

paper.title: Machine Learning-Based Prediction of Disease-Free Survival in Breast Cancer Incorporating Clinical and Treatment Information: Retrospective Cohort Study With External Validation.
paper.abstract:
Background: Breast cancer is the most prevalent cancer in women, and postoperative disease-free survival (DFS) is an important indicator of long-term prognosis. However, tumor, node, metastasis staging has limited ability to integrate multidimensional clinical, pathological, and treatment-related factors for individualized DFS prediction. Therefore, machine learning (ML) may provide a more comprehensive approach to prognostic risk assessment.
Objective: This study aimed to develop and externally validate a ML-based model for predicting postoperative DFS in patients with breast cancer.
Methods: This retrospective study included 2 cohorts: 1231 patients treated at an institutional center between 2012 and 2020 and 304 patients from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA). The institutional cohort was divided into model development (n=861) and internal validation (n=370) sets, while the TCGA cohort served as an external validation cohort. Five ML algorithms were evaluated, with the Cox proportional hazards model additionally fitted as a conventional statistical reference. Model performance was assessed using the concordance index and time-dependent area under the curve (AUC). The net reclassification index and integrated discrimination improvement were used for comparative evaluation. Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) analysis was performed to assess predictor contributions, and patients were stratified into risk groups according to the median predicted risk score.
Results: Based on a comprehensive evaluation of model performance, extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) with an accelerated failure time (AFT) was selected as the final model. The study included 1231 institutional patients, with 861 used for model development and 370 for internal validation, and 304 patients from TCGA for external validation. The 5-year time-dependent AUCs were 0.840, 0.822, and 0.762 in the training, internal validation, and external validation cohorts, respectively. In the external validation cohort, the XGBoost (AFT) model achieved a concordance index of 0.750 (95% CI 0.654-0.843), with 3-, 5-, and 8-year AUCs of 0.791, 0.762, and 0.768, respectively. At 5 years, compared with Cox regression, XGBoost (AFT) showed improved reclassification (net reclassification index=0.311, 95% CI 0.172-0.458; P=.01; integrated discrimination improvement=0.166, 95% CI 0.095-0.235; P<.001). SHAP analysis identified endocrine therapy, pT, pN, lymph node ratio, Ki-67, and chemotherapy among the major contributors to model predictions. Risk stratification based on the median predicted risk score separated patients into groups with distinct DFS outcomes (hazard ratio 5.44, 95% CI 4.04-7.31).
Conclusions: The ML-based model demonstrated favorable performance and external generalizability in predicting postoperative DFS. SHAP analysis provided interpretability for the model, and risk stratification identified patient subgroups with distinct prognostic risks.
